processing: Made the way Phoenix dancong usually is: sun-withered, shaken and rested in rounds, then fixed, rolled and dried, with the roast set by the maker.
harvest_season: As with most Phoenix dancong, the spring picking is the main and most prized one.
appearance_dry: Large, sturdy strands, grey-brown with an oily sheen.
appearance_wet: Large leaves with reddened edges, as is usual for well-shaken dancong.
taste_profile: A long honey scent over a thick, sweet and smooth body, with the lingering mountain character people call shan yun.

brewing.notes: General dancong approach: very hot water and quick pours. Its large strands fill the gaiwan fast, so judge by weight, not by eye.

vintage_note: Usually sold like other Phoenix dancong: by spring harvest of the current year, often after a roast and a rest, with older roasted stock marked by year. It is rarely seen under its own name outside China, so ask the village.
description:
She Men is a Phoenix Mountain dancong named after a place. The first character, 輋, is a rare regional one, and you may see the name romanised in different ways.

The usual account puts it in the honey-orchid family. It is known for a big, sturdy, grey-brown leaf with an oily sheen. One vendor's list instead files a 輋门 tree under miscellaneous clear-fragrance, so don't treat the family as completely settled.

The cup is described as thick and sweet, with a long honey scent and a clear mountain character, and it holds up well over many steeps. Brew it hot and fast like any dancong, and let the later steeps go longer.

Generic Mi Lan Xiang is easier to find than a true She Men. Trying the two side by side is the quickest way to learn what the name adds.
history: Little is documented about its age or selection. A Chinese tea science overview lists it among lines named after places, and it is named in lists of notable Wudong trees. One vendor's list places a tree of this name in Hucuo, Wudong Village.
